You previously formulated the following research problem for the target paper.

Research problem: In MVFA's few-shot setting the image-level anomaly score is formed by adding a zero-shot softmax probability in [0, 1] to a few-shot memory-bank cosine distance in [0, 2] with a fixed weight of 0.5, and by taking the maximum over pixels; can a label-free, support-set-based normalisation of the two branch scores — standardising each branch's score against its own leave-one-out score distribution on the K normal support images — combined with a robust image-level aggregation (top-k mean or high-quantile pooling instead of the maximum), produce a fused anomaly score whose single operating threshold transfers across unseen modalities? The measurable outcomes are expected calibration error, sensitivity at 95% specificity and F1 at a threshold fixed before seeing any target label, alongside image-level AUROC, compared with MVFA's original fusion on every held-out BMAD modality.
Rationale: Limitations G8, G9 and G11 share one root cause: MVFA's scores are only ever evaluated by threshold-free AUC, so the fact that its two branches live on different scales, that one branch can dominate the sum, and that a single spurious pixel decides the image label is invisible in the reported results — yet a deployed detector must commit to a threshold. The related literature focuses almost entirely on representation (adapters in MLCA, ClipMPCAD and Adaptive Feature Fusion; prompts in AnomalyCLIP, HieClip and the text-adapted few-shot framework); AnomalyGPT is the only related work that explicitly removes manual thresholds, and it does so with a large vision-language model and supervised fine-tuning rather than with a principled treatment of scores. The few-shot setting offers an under-used resource: the K normal support images themselves define what "normal" scores look like for each branch in the new modality, which makes per-modality standardisation possible without any target labels. The problem is fine-grained — it touches only the score-fusion and aggregation step, so the backbone and adapters are unchanged and existing MVFA checkpoints can be reused — and it is cheap to investigate on a single GPU because it requires inference only. Requiring thresholded, calibration-aware metrics under the modality-disjoint, multi-seed and multi-draw protocol directly addresses the evaluation gaps, since few-shot support draws are exactly where score scales vary most.

ReviewingAgents evaluated it on five criteria. Their reviews, feedback, and ratings are:
- Clarity: rating 4/5. Review: The defect being fixed is described precisely (scales [0,1] and [0,2], fixed weight 0.5, max pooling), and the outcomes are concrete (ECE, sensitivity at 95% specificity, F1 at a pre-fixed threshold, AUROC). However, the problem bundles two interventions — branch normalisation and aggregation — and it is not stated which is the primary question. Feedback: Make the primary question the transferability of a single threshold, and frame normalisation and robust pooling as the two factors of a 2x2 design so their individual effects are identifiable. State how the 'threshold fixed before seeing any target label' is chosen (on source modalities? on support normals?).
- Relevance: rating 4/5. Review: Directly addresses G8, G9 and G11 of the target paper and the general lack of thresholded evaluation in the related CLIP-based anomaly detection works. Relevant to anyone deploying few-shot detectors. Feedback: Connect explicitly to score normalisation practice in PatchCore-style methods and to AnomalyGPT's threshold-free claim.
- Originality: rating 3/5. Review: Score standardisation before fusion (z-normalisation) is a classical technique, and robust pooling such as top-k mean is common in anomaly detection. The genuinely fresh part is using leave-one-out scores on the K normal support images as a label-free per-modality reference and evaluating threshold transfer, which most papers in this area ignore. Feedback: Put the threshold-transfer question and the leave-one-out support reference at the centre to make the contribution clearly distinct from generic normalisation.
- Feasibility: rating 5/5. Review: Inference-only on existing MVFA checkpoints; all quantities are computable from BMAD labels; the multi-seed, multi-draw protocol is cheap because no retraining is needed. Feedback: None significant; ensure that K normal support images exist for K=2 (the leave-one-out distribution from two images is degenerate — consider pooling patch-level scores).
- Significance: rating 3/5. Review: A practical improvement for deployment of few-shot detectors, but restricted to the few-shot regime and to score post-processing; the contribution to the field is useful but narrow. Feedback: Broaden the significance by showing that the same normalisation makes MVFA comparable with other few-shot methods at fixed operating points, or that it changes conclusions drawn from AUROC alone.

Revise the research problem so that it addresses the feedback while keeping what the reviewers rated highly. Keep it a single, fine-grained, to-the-point problem that still addresses the same limitations, respects the constraints below, and stays centred on the target paper.

Target paper title: Adapting Visual-Language Models for Generalizable Anomaly Detection in Medical Images
Target paper abstract: Recent advancements in large-scale visual-language pre-trained models have led to significant progress in zero-/few-shot anomaly detection within natural image domains. However, the substantial domain divergence between natural and medical images limits the effectiveness of these methodologies in medical anomaly detection. This paper introduces a novel lightweight multi-level adaptation and comparison framework to repurpose the CLIP model for medical anomaly detection. Our approach integrates multiple residual adapters into the pre-trained visual encoder, enabling a stepwise enhancement of visual features across different levels. This multi-level adaptation is guided by multi-level, pixel-wise visual-language feature alignment loss functions, which recalibrate the model's focus from object semantics in natural imagery to anomaly identification in medical images. The adapted features exhibit improved generalization across various medical data types, even in zero-shot scenarios where the model encounters unseen medical modalities and anatomical regions during training. Our experiments on medical anomaly detection benchmarks demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art models, with an average AUC improvement of 6.24% and 7.33% for anomaly classification, 2.03% and 2.37% for anomaly segmentation, under the zero-shot and few-shot settings, respectively. Source code is available at: https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD
Limitations to address:
- G8. Architecture, fusion, and hyperparameters are under-ablated and partly unclear: Numerous design choices — including γ = 0.1, λ = 1.0, four feature levels, an input resolution of 240, a learning rate of 10−3, a batch size of 16, 50 training epochs, β = 0.5, and fixed prompt templates — are presented without accompanying sensitivity analysis. The adapter and projector equations and their class-token handling are dimensionally unclear, and the partitioning of the 24-layer Vision Transformer into four stages is non-standard, which hinders reproducibility. The final score fusion combines zero-shot softmax probabilities on the interval [0, 1] with few-shot cosine distances on the interval [0, 2] using a fixed weight of 0.5, without normalization or calibration, so that one branch may arbitrarily dominate the fused score.
- G9. Classification and aggregation are outlier-sensitive: Image-level anomaly classification is obtained via max-aggregation over pixel-level anomaly scores, so that a single spurious high-scoring pixel is sufficient to produce a false positive. No robust aggregation, calibration, or uncertainty-estimation mechanism is employed to mitigate this sensitivity.
- G11. Metrics are too narrow for clinical readiness: Only image-level and pixel-level AUC are reported. The paper does not report Dice, IoU, or PRO scores; thresholded accuracy, F1, sensitivity, specificity, PPV, or NPV; false positives per patient; calibration or expected calibration error (ECE); or prevalence-adjusted and rare-category performance. AUC alone can obscure poor performance under severe class imbalance and does not by itself demonstrate clinical utility.
Constraints:
- The problem will be investigated by a student team in the next few weeks by modifying the public code of the target paper (https://github.com/MediaBrain-SJTU/MVFA-AD) and evaluating on the public BMAD benchmark (brain MRI, liver CT, retinal OCT: RESC and OCT17, chest X-ray, histopathology), using a single Google Colab Pro GPU (A100 40GB or L4 24GB). No new clinical data can be collected and no new expert annotations can be made.
- Shared evaluation protocol (from limitation group C: G2, G10, G12): results must be reported under a modality-disjoint leave-one-modality-out split (RESC and OCT17 are held out together, never one with the other in training), with patient-level separation where identifiers exist, over at least 3 random seeds and 3 few-shot support draws with mean and standard deviation, and against the missing baselines named in G12 where relevant.

Problem: Can a single anomaly threshold, chosen without any target labels, transfer to unseen modalities in MVFA's few-shot setting? MVFA's image score adds a zero-shot softmax probability in [0, 1] to a memory-bank cosine distance in [0, 2] with weight 0.5 and max-pools over pixels. We study a 2x2 design: (factor 1) branch scores raw versus standardised by each branch's leave-one-out patch-score distribution on the K normal support images (each support image's patches scored against the memory bank built from the other K-1 images, pooled over patches so that K = 2 is non-degenerate); (factor 2) max pooling versus top-k-mean pooling. In every cell the threshold is set as the 95th percentile of the support leave-one-out image scores. Outcomes: realised specificity and sensitivity at that threshold, F1, expected calibration error and image-level AUROC on every held-out BMAD modality, for K in {2, 4, 8, 16}, under the modality-disjoint, 3-seed, 3-draw protocol.

Rationale: The reviewers asked for one primary question, an explicit threshold rule, a fix for the K = 2 degeneracy and separable factors. The primary question is now threshold transfer; the support-set leave-one-out distribution supplies both the normalisation statistics and the threshold, which is the label-free element that distinguishes this from generic z-score fusion; the 2x2 design identifies the separate effects of normalisation and aggregation. Showing whether conclusions drawn from AUROC alone change at fixed operating points broadens the significance beyond MVFA. The study is inference-only on public MVFA checkpoints and therefore cheap to run across all seeds and draws.
